apps.name: Octave
apps.subtitle: Free, full-quality music streaming.
apps.localizedDescription:
Octave is a full-quality music player for iPhone and iPad.

• Full-length streaming up to lossless
• Offline downloads
• Word-by-word karaoke lyrics
• Sing — real vocal separation, not just centre-channel cancellation
• Home-Screen and Lock-Screen widgets, Control Centre controls and Siri
• Listening parties, collaborative playlists and public profiles
• Podcasts from Apple's own catalogue

Not on the App Store. Sideload it and sign it with your own Apple ID.

A note on widgets. Top Charts, Made For You and Live Radio work on every install — they read the catalogue directly and need nothing from the app. Now Playing, Recently Played and Pinned show what you're actually listening to, which reaches them through an App Group.

An App Group belongs permanently to the team that first registered it, so your signing tool has to rewrite Octave's to one your own Apple ID owns. This is not about paid versus free — a paid account hits the same wall. AltStore and SideStore rewrite it for you, and TrollStore skips the question entirely, so all six widgets work on those. In Sideloadly, turn on "Change Bundle ID", or signing fails before it starts. Never turn on "Remove app extensions" — that deletes the widgets outright.

If those three widgets read "Widget data is locked", your signer dropped the group instead of rewriting it. The other three keep working regardless.

versions.localizedDescription: The first play of a song nobody had played yet failed on iPhone: the server sent the whole file without honouring the byte ranges iOS asks for, and iOS refuses that for lossless, Atmos and AAC files. The server now answers those requests the way iOS expects, so a never-played song starts in a few seconds instead of failing. Worse, after one failure like that the player itself could stop accepting songs — even files already on your phone — until the app was quit; it is now replaced with a fresh one the moment it holds a failed song, and a player that says "playing" while holding nothing is rebuilt within seconds at the same position. A failed switch to Dolby Atmos or to a new quality no longer skips the song that was playing fine, the connections used for playback time out and are rebuilt after a long idle or a switch between Wi-Fi and cellular, and the next song no longer tries to preload before your playback token is ready. Next and Previous now change the title, artwork and lock screen on the tap and silence the old song straight away; with AutoMix on, the next song is preloaded again. Covers are downloaded once per song, retried when a connection drops, fetched through Octave's servers when Apple's or Deezer's image servers refuse, and loaded again as soon as the network or the app comes back — a cover that fails no longer leaves the previous song's cover in its place. Downloads keep going through iOS dropping the download service, force-quits and brief previews, with longer pauses between retries. Add a folder uses Apple's folder picker, reads the folder the way Apple documents, downloads songs still in iCloud first, and says what went wrong when it can't.

An artist's station is built once an hour and shared by every listener, which is right for the recommendations that read it but wrong for pressing ▶: the station played top-down, so it opened on the same song for everyone until the hour turned over. Starting a station now asks for its own deal of that list — the first song is one of the artist's own, drawn from their best-known tracks, and the rest is reshuffled with the strongest picks still leaning early and no act playing twice in a row. This covers the artist page, album and playlist Radio, the Radio tab, concerts and the artist menu. Also in this build, from 7.3: playlist imports from TuneMyMusic or Exportify no longer report songs as missing when the catalog was only rate-limiting the lookups, a whole-library export can be kept as separate playlists, Next works on stations again, "& Similar Artists" starts on a new song each time, and the iPhone app stays in portrait.

Importing a playlist file matched songs to the catalog many at once, ran into the catalog's rate limit within seconds, and reported every refused lookup as a song Octave doesn't have; on top of that, the catalog's search had quietly stopped honouring artist names, so the rest fell back to a loose search that preferred remixes. The server side of this was fixed first and already helps older builds. This build sends the file in smaller pieces, asks again for anything the server didn't get to, and tells you apart the songs the catalog doesn't have from the ones that simply couldn't be checked — import again and those are picked up. The CSV reader handles quoted line breaks, Excel and Numbers encodings and the runtime column, and a TuneMyMusic whole-library backup can be kept as separate playlists, merged into one, or narrowed to a single playlist. Choosing the file now uses the system picker with a copied file, which fixes the CSV that couldn't be selected when the importer was opened from Settings and files still sitting in iCloud. On stations, Next was refused whenever a station was playing — the rule meant for live radio caught every station — so only scrubbing to the end or tapping the queue moved on; it advances again, live broadcasts excepted. "& Similar Artists" is built on the device now and starts somewhere new each time instead of on the same song. Finally, the iPhone app no longer rotates to landscape, where the tab bar and Now Playing were drawn half off-screen; iPad still rotates.

The AutoMix engine used to arm a transition on the song that was already playing — a new audio mix, a filter schedule and a tempo ramp written onto the live item a few seconds in. On an iPhone every one of those writes is a short gap in the sound, and a queue edit made it happen three times in a row. Each upcoming song is now created with both its incoming and its own outgoing transition already declared; when its seam arrives the engine writes only the advance time and the end time, and the live song is left alone. If the plan changes underneath, the queued song is rebuilt (free) rather than the live one; only when a song was never created with its window does the old live write run, and it says so in the log. The arm also waits for the record after next to be analysed and for Sound Check loudness to land, so the declared windows carry the right level. Separately, a song whose stream died and whose replacement never loaded — status unknown, no bytes, the player reporting nothing to play — kept spinning: each tap of play re-asserted the dead item, and each pause cancelled the rescue timer. Play now rebuilds the song from a fresh source when the player says it has nothing to play, or on the second tap on the same dead item, and the stall watchdog does the same after its nudge. Also in this build, from 7.1: Repeat One keeps the looping song instead of downloading it again every lap, a deck that fails once is rebuilt instead of skipping your song, animations run at 120 Hz on ProMotion, closing the player keeps your finger's momentum, hidden controls come back before the lyrics page folds, and Settings is readable on light themes.

Two things made a song jump in its first minute. With Repeat One on and a transition set, the song about to loop back was never kept on the device, so every lap pulled the full file down again onto the second deck while the song was playing — that was the stutter right before the second verse. The song is now cached once and the loop stages the file. Separately, editing the queue while AutoMix had a transition planned made the mixer restore the live song's audio mix and then write a new one straight after; on a phone every one of those writes is a short dropout. The restore now waits a moment and is skipped when a new plan replaces it. Skipping quickly through an album could leave a song that refused to load — even one already downloaded. A deck that had failed once (a Dolby Atmos pull that never arrived) was left unable to start anything, and because the other deck kept working the rebuild that exists for this never fired. Failures are now counted per deck, and a deck that cannot start a local file triggers the rebuild at once instead of skipping the song. Every animation had been capped at 60 Hz on ProMotion iPhones; the Now Playing fold, the lyric springs and the transitions now run at 120 Hz. Closing the player keeps your finger's momentum after you let go and then folds the cover into the bar, the way Apple Music does. On Lyrics and Queue, when the controls have hidden themselves and you tap the artwork, the controls come back first and then the page folds — it used to snap. Settings on a light theme was unreadable, dark cards with dark text; the cards are white on the theme's page colour now.

Album pages behind a dark cover were painted a colour that appears nowhere in the artwork. The page keeps light covers from glaring by darkening them to a fixed level, which is what Apple Music does — but the same rule also worked in reverse, brightening dark covers by up to four times and turning anything close to black into flat grey. So Heroes & Villains, black with purple flames, sat on a teal page, and When We All Fall Asleep, Where Do We Go? sat on grey. The rule now only ever darkens: a dark cover keeps its own colour, and both of those albums now paint exactly the colour Apple Music publishes for them. Light covers are unchanged.

Coming from 6.4.1? This build also carries everything in 7.0: Search works again on iOS 27, cards in the New tab respond to taps, AutoMix blends on a phone instead of cutting, Apple's redesigned artist pages, Siri can open your library by name, and Podcasts is rebuilt.

iOS 27 arrived and took three things with it. Search opened to a page with no search field anywhere on it — Octave had never drawn its own, because iOS 26 lets the tab bar supply one, and 27 stopped creating the container that holds it. Cards in the New tab were dead to taps: the route they carried was type-erased, and the system matches a link to its destination on the exact type, so nothing happened and nothing was logged. And the mini player stopped tucking into the tab bar, because a guard written against an early 27 beta was still switching the behaviour off on the finished release. All three are fixed, and the first two are now covered by tests that fail loudly rather than quietly.

Two older bugs went with them. Pressing next sometimes did nothing and sometimes took the app down, which turned out to be two threads tearing down the same audio unit at the same moment. Lyrics drifted behind the music because the lyric clock was subtracting a delay that only applies when Sing is switched on — with Sing off, every transition pulled the words out of step.

AutoMix is the substantial change. Apple's beat-matched styles hold the volume almost flat and carry the audible fade in a filter instead, and that filter was being described to the audio engine but never actually scheduled — so on a phone every beat-matched transition was a hard cut, and had been for as long as the native engine has been in use. Transitions now run their full window, Dolby Atmos tracks get the same treatment where before they carried no mix at all, and AutoMix refuses cleanly with Apple's own wording when a transition genuinely cannot run.

Artist pages are rebuilt to Apple's current design — the artist's own logo and colour, the four header treatments, and Apple's section order — and the play button now starts that artist's station rather than a fixed list of their top songs. Siri can open things by name rather than only play them: albums, artists, playlists, stations, mixes and library sections, including Liked Songs, On Repeat, Made For You and Downloaded. Opening no longer starts playback. Podcasts is rebuilt to match Podcasts on macOS 27, with playback speed as its own setting, remembered per show and no longer leaking into music.

Smaller, and worth having: shuffle starts a genuinely fresh lap when Repeat All comes round, full-screen lyrics with the media controls fading out the way Apple's do while the artwork and heart stay put, the Now Playing colour no longer keeping the previous song's palette, and Apple's play triangle redrawn with the rounded corners it actually has. Measured on both iOS 26.5 and 27: no state in the app costs more on 27 than on 26.5, and neither version throttles.

With AutoMix on, Repeat One was ignored. Apple's mixing engine is handed the next record well before the end, and that hand-over was built from the queue position rather than the repeat mode — so the next song was inserted behind the one playing and the player advanced to it at the seam. Repeat One now blends the song into its own start, as it always did on the two-deck path, and a hand-over that was already armed comes down the moment you switch AutoMix off or change the repeat mode, instead of playing out under the new setting. Separately, with AutoMix off, the restart itself could hang: the player drops a finished song from its queue, so the rewind pointed at nothing and playback sat silent until a 20-second watchdog reloaded the file. Under Repeat One the finished song now stays in place and restarts at once. A duplicate end notification that could trigger a second restart is also ignored.

This release finishes the AutoMix work. The style selector is Apple's iOS 27 catalogue walked as data — eight strategies, a genre gate read off Apple's own tables, and the decoded danceability and acousticness thresholds — so a hip-hop pair, a dance pair and a pop pair each get the mix Apple would give them, and a pair Apple refuses to beat-match is joined rather than forced. Dead-air joins open exactly where the outgoing record goes dark; a song that opens quietly over a long silent tail gets Apple's smart cross-fade, entering on the bar before it gets loud. Seeking near a planned mix follows the four rules Music.app logs: a seek before the open keeps the plan, a seek at or past it voids it and re-plans behind Apple's 10.5 s safety margin. The exit law sits on the authored grid, the Mixing badge comes down when the outgoing has actually left, the deck path's 0.26 s hole at the seam is closed, and the watchdog that fired a mix far too early stands down. Apple's six iOS 27 genre styles are transcribed lane for lane with their AURemixFX effects rack; on iOS 26 they play as the closest iOS 26 style, exactly as Apple's iOS 26 does.

Lyrics: with Sing engaged the vocal isolator adds roughly 0.65 s of latency, and the lyrics were running that far ahead of the voice you heard — the lyric clock now subtracts the live render latency, measured at 0 ms on the phone. Lines change on their cue rather than on a 6 Hz timer, blurred lines wrap at the column, and Japanese lyrics carry a pronunciation guide.

Sound Check follows Apple Music's law as read from AudioToolboxCore: a loud master is cut in full with no floor, a quiet one is lifted only within the headroom under −1 dBTP and never past +20 dB, and an album is levelled by its loudest track so a quiet song on a loud record stays quiet. App and website now apply the same correction to the same song.

Also in 6.4: the equaliser is Apple Music's — ten bands, Apple's 22 presets and a ±12 dB preamp; recommendations run on-device with the same engine as the website and Autoplay fills the queue without a server call; the Shuffle chip cycles off, Shuffle and Smart Shuffle; the heart pops like the web's; Library lists keep their order on name ties and sort descending correctly; pre-order albums show Apple's "Coming <date>" badge; a sleep timer lives in the ⋯ menu; Clear Queue asks first; resuming after a long pause rebuilds the stream instead of failing; search shows "Showing results for…" when it corrected you; and motion covers play by Apple's rule.

Fixes the iOS 27 bug that made the app feel frozen, and four Auto-Mix defects: a mix that ran 7% long, a stutter on first-time songs, a badge that announced itself before anything happened, and beat-matching against the wrong master on Dolby Atmos.

Auto-Mix was rebuilt against Apple Music's own transition table, read out of iOS 26, iOS 27 and macOS. Every blend now follows Apple's real gain curves and bar-length windows instead of an approximation, and the transitions no longer break. Five faults were found and fixed by measuring the two decks directly, on a phone, with Dolby Atmos and AirPods: a two-second stall on every Atmos transition, a quarter-second of the new song's start being swallowed by the fade, a failed Atmos stream that stopped the next track from ever being ready, songs being cut several seconds short when the next one was still loading, and a four-second mute a few seconds after each mix. Dolby Atmos also now engages on songs the queue mixes into, not only ones you tap.

Search by the line stuck in your head. Type a lyric — "I been tryna call", "hello darkness my old friend" — and Octave finds the song, then shows you the line with the matched words picked out. It searches the words, not the titles, so if what you typed is a song's name it tells you that instead of pretending it found nothing. Tapping a result plays that one song rather than loading forty covers of it behind you.

Auto-Mix now has a real DJ rack. Blends were a crossfade with a bass swap; they can now loop a bar back on itself, throw a delay, open and close a filter, and stop the outgoing record like tape. Every rate is locked to the beat rather than a stopwatch — the delay time is derived from the outgoing track's own beat, so the same effect on a 122 BPM record and a 128 BPM record produces two different delay lengths, each exactly three-quarters of that song's beat. Nothing fires on a pair it would spoil: a track that can't be beat-matched gets a filtered exit instead of a smear, and the whole rack costs about two per cent of one audio thread.

Auto-Mix also works properly on AirPods now. It had been quietly collapsing to a four-second fade on any wireless output — no beat-matching, no bass swap — and the badge even said "Crossfading" while Auto-Mix was on and working. That restriction is gone, on Bluetooth and AirPlay alike. And a mix can no longer go silent in the middle: the outgoing song is now held until the incoming one has actually made a sound, which on one measured transition was worth 1.77 seconds of silence that simply isn't there any more.

Credits are Apple's now. Every person, every role they played — including the engineers, who were missing entirely — and a photo for each one, grouped the way Apple groups them: performing artists, composition and lyrics, production and engineering.

Album pages gained three things: Featured On, the editorial playlists a record appears in; You Might Also Like; and the ★ on the songs that matter most, using the real popularity figure and the same 0.7 threshold Apple uses rather than our own guess.

Elsewhere: Library ▸ Songs and the Liked Songs tile now open the same screen instead of two different ones. Every Library page says what it will search — "Search Albums", "Search Artists" — and you can drag a song, album or playlist onto the mini player to queue it. Pins gained an edit screen. Playlist tiles no longer run off the right edge of narrower phones.

And a lot of this release is for people on older iPhones. On iOS 18 the album and artist pages had no navigation bar at all, so scrolling content ran straight through the title and the clock; and the mini player never reserved its space, leaving the last inch of every list unreachable on every tab. Both are fixed.

This is the largest release Octave has had, and almost all of it is the player.

Now Playing used to be a sheet that slid up over the app. It is now a zoom: the artwork you tapped grows into the player and folds back down into the row or the mini-player it came from, one picture the whole way, the way Apple Music does it. Getting there meant removing as much as adding — the bounce at the end of the close, the second cover that flashed through the dismiss, the sleeve dissolve, the bar's spring-up beat, and the mask that briefly showed the previous track's artwork are all deleted rather than tuned. The title block can no longer land on top of the scrubber, the close arrives instead of being cut off, and switching between a square sleeve and a full-bleed immersive poster is a single shape flip instead of two covers arguing.

Sing does genuine vocal separation now, not centre-channel cancellation, so the backing track survives while the vocal comes down — and it works on Dolby Atmos tracks, which it silently refused to do before. Lyrics translate on-device: free, offline, nothing leaves the phone. Background vocals sit back in their own weight, and a lyric line can no longer keep scrolling past the end of the song it was written for.

Auto-Mix gained a picker — Automatic, Apple's timing, or Octave's — and the badge now names the transition that is actually happening rather than the one that was planned. The queue, the credits sheet, the song context menu and Add to Playlist were all rebuilt to match Apple's structure, so Up Next has its History section, credits list people by role, and the menu is flat sections in a fixed order instead of a scrolling stack.

Widgets are the other headline. Now Playing, Recently Played and Pins read your library through an App Group, and an App Group belongs permanently to the team that registered it — so on a sideloaded copy those three used to say "Widget data is locked". They now reach your phone through Octave's own relay instead, and all six widgets work on an ordinary install.

The rest is weight and correctness. The player's backdrop stopped redrawing under your finger, a hidden lyric panel stopped running a 30-times-a-second clock behind the queue, and the Home tab stopped rebuilding itself on every frame of a drag. A 500-song playlist went from hitching on 27.7% of frames to none. Album, Playlist and Library were rebuilt to their measured layouts. Recommendations learn from what you actually listen to, on-device. Octave runs on iOS 18 again, with its own chrome for the older layout. And a long list of fixes underneath: skipping back no longer hangs, downloads no longer wedge behind a dead background session, explicit songs stop playing the clean master, changing quality mid-song keeps your place, playlist sharing actually publishes, a large library stops silently failing to sync, and the #1 song on Home is the one from your part of the world.
Minor bug fixes and improvements.
Shuffle now survives a restart. Close Octave with shuffle on and it is still on when you come back — the queue keeps its shuffled order instead of quietly resetting to off.

Search for a song, tap it, and Octave used to load every other result behind it as your queue. For a well-known song that means a wall of covers, karaoke uploads, live bootlegs and sped-up edits — thirty-odd recordings of the same title by people you never searched for — and autoplay, the thing that is supposed to follow a song with music that actually relates to it, did not get a turn until every one of them had played. The queue said so out loud: "From Search · 38 queued". A result list is a ranked guess, not a lineup, so it is no longer treated as one. Tapping a search result plays that song and hands what comes next to autoplay, the same way playing a song from anywhere else in the app has always worked. Albums, playlists and mixes are untouched — those genuinely are collections, and they still play straight through. Asking Siri or Shortcuts to play something got the same fix, since it was queueing forty matches while telling you it had played one. And songs that autoplay adds to any queue are now labelled as autoplay's, so Up Next stops attributing a radio to whatever album or playlist you happened to start from.

If you have ever tapped Import Loved tracks and watched Octave add a couple of dozen songs from a list of over a thousand, this is the release that fixes it. The import was asking the server for a shelf — a short, cached list meant for a discovery row — and then reporting whatever came back as the whole job. Thirty songs went out, one was a duplicate, twenty-nine landed in your library, and nothing anywhere said the other nine hundred and seventy had been left behind. The import now enumerates your complete Loved list once and works through it in batches, showing you how far along it is, and it keeps going until it has actually finished. Everything else in this build is unchanged.

This release is about one thing: downloading a whole album or playlist and actually getting it. Octave handed iOS a few songs at a time and kept the rest of the queue in memory only. iOS suspends and then terminates apps in the background constantly — that is normal, not a crash — and every time it did, the songs still waiting were gone. Nothing told you. The album just sat there part-saved, and starting it again only re-queued the same handful. That is why 'downloads don't work' for so many people, and why it looked random: it depended entirely on when your phone decided to close the app. The queue is now written to disk as you go. When iOS wakes Octave — because a download finished, or because you opened it again — it reads what it still owes you and hands the next batch straight to the system downloader, which keeps running whether Octave is open or not. Kill the app mid-download as many times as you like; the album finishes. Anything left half-saved by older versions is repaired on your next launch instead of being retried forever. Two smaller fixes ride along: downloads now save at the Download quality you chose in Settings, rather than inheriting whatever quality your connection was on at that moment, and songs that aren't available in Lossless are saved under the format they really are, so they open properly instead of being re-downloaded on every launch.

For about two and a half hours yesterday afternoon, one connection pulled roughly forty-five thousand full-quality tracks out of Octave by pretending to be Deezer's own bandwidth tester. Nobody's account or library was touched, and nothing was lost. What it did take was capacity: Octave fetches a song nobody has played yet using a shared, finite set of accounts, and while that run was going, tens of thousands of songs other people asked for came back as thirty-second previews because there was nothing left to fetch them with. Octave already had a ceiling on how much music it pulls fresh in a day, and that ceiling held — the problem was that a single caller was allowed to spend the whole thing. There is now a second ceiling on how much any one connection can pull, set roughly twenty times higher than a heavy day of listening, so a real listener will never notice it while a sweep of the catalogue runs out of room in short order. Separately, the pass your app holds to play audio now lasts two hours instead of twelve, which shortens the window if one ever leaks. This build is the half of that change that lives on your phone: the old app assumed every pass came with an hour of slack, and a shorter pass does not, which would have surfaced as songs quietly refusing to start and downloads stopping partway. It now renews in proportion to however long the pass actually lasts. There is nothing to do on your end.

Downloads were repaired a couple of releases ago, but the repair could not reach the people who most needed it. When a download failed, Octave put that song on a cooldown that widened each time it happened, up to a full day, and it kept that list across updates. So anyone who collected cooldowns while downloads were broken carried them straight into the fixed version: automatic downloads kept skipping those songs, and installing the update looked like it changed nothing at all. This build clears that list once, on first launch. A song that genuinely is not available will earn its cooldown back on the next attempt, one attempt at a time, so nothing gets hammered — it simply gets a fair first try under code that works. Elsewhere: a listening party no longer drops someone who is still in the room when their connection blips, which is what left two devices disagreeing about how many people were listening; clearing your queue twice now deals a different set of songs instead of the same lineup; a Spotify import longer than three hundred songs resolves all the way to the end rather than stopping there; a podcast episode that refuses to play says whether it is behind a subscription or blocked by its host, instead of being skipped in silence; and a track that is provably still downloading gets the time it needs before Octave suggests something has gone wrong.

Shows you like now have somewhere to live. Open any podcast and tap Follow, and it lands in Your Library under a new Podcasts section — no more digging through search or charts to find the one you were halfway through. You can follow straight from a show's tile too, by holding it anywhere shows appear. Following syncs the same way the rest of your library does, so a show you follow on the web is already there on your phone, and unfollowing on one device removes it everywhere instead of quietly coming back on the next sync.

Saving music while listening was quietly failing. Playback and downloads share one budget on the server, and when a busy moment made it ask for a pause, downloads waited about seven seconds before writing the song off — so a track that was perfectly fine came back as "Couldn't download", and sat out a fifteen-minute cooldown for it. Octave now waits as long as the server actually asks, and the whole queue eases off together instead of every song racing to fail. Separately, the very first download after installing the app, or after a day away from it, could go out without credentials and fail on the spot; it no longer can.

Some episodes are only available to Apple Podcasts subscribers, and a few shows are hosted somewhere that refuses our servers. Both used to fail the same way — the episode was skipped with a vague message, or no message at all, which made it look like Octave was broken. The real reason is now shown instead.

If the host refreshed the page, switched devices, or just hit a brief network blip, the party was being torn down behind the scenes — everyone was dropped and the room showed nobody listening. The host reconnecting is now treated as what it is, and the listener list is sent from the server as a whole rather than pieced together from join and leave events, so every device agrees on who is in the room.

Large playlist imports were silently cut off at 300 songs — and the app reported the smaller number as the total, so nothing ever said songs had been dropped. Files, exports and Spotify links now import in full, however long the playlist is.

A track that had aged out of the streaming cache is rebuilt from cold storage, which can take longer than ten seconds to hand over its first note. The player counted that as a dead track and skipped it — even though the download was healthy and on its way. Now it watches whether audio is actually still arriving, and only gives up on a track that has genuinely stopped moving. A song that will not start also gets one fresh attempt before it is passed over.

Volume normalization has been wrong since the day it shipped, and this release fixes it. Deezer publishes a number alongside every track that is named like a ReplayGain correction but is not one — it is a measurement of the track's integrated loudness, and it is negative for every song in the catalogue. Octave applied it verbatim to the output, which meant a track ended up at twice its own loudness below reference rather than at the target. Masters that already sat near the target came out about right, and since virtually all modern pop is mastered into that narrow band, the feature looked like it worked. Anything outside it did not: a 1962 live recording measured at -19 LUFS was being driven down to -33, roughly 19 dB quieter than where YouTube Music plays the same recording, and the only thing that stopped it going further was a floor in the code. The correction is now calculated from the measurement rather than mistaken for one, verified against ffmpeg's loudness meter across a 25 dB span of real tracks. The reference level moved too, from Apple Music's -16 LUFS to the -14 that Spotify, Tidal and YouTube Music all use, because that is what people are actually comparing against.

That same mistake explains the other half of what people were reporting: a song that started at a sensible volume and then sank a few seconds in. Two systems set playback level — a live meter that listens to the audio as it plays, and the track's own loudness data, which arrives shortly after playback begins. The meter was arriving at the right answer and the data was then overruling it with the wrong one. Both now aim at the same reference, so a track holds its level when one hands over to the other.

Your public profile is no longer buried. It lived in a card inside Settings, which meant that on a phone there was no reasonable way to open your own page, copy its link, or send it to anybody — you had to know the URL and type it. Tapping your avatar now puts My Profile at the top of the menu, under your name and handle, with Copy Profile Link and Share Profile next to it. If you haven't claimed a username or haven't made your profile public, that row takes you to the screen where you can, rather than to a page that would tell you it doesn't exist.

Two smaller things. On Now Playing, the album name printed under the artwork was inert, even though the identical album name lower down the same screen opened the album — the one you reach for first now does what it looks like it does. And Octave's bundle identifier and App Group are now a single setting in Octave.xcconfig, so if you build the app yourself under your own Apple ID you change one line instead of eleven scattered across the project, the entitlements and the source.

There is nothing new to look at in this one. It exists because a widget that isn't working looks identical whether it is running the newest build or a stale one, and on a sideloaded install a stale build is a real possibility: the update may not have applied, or a widget placed before the app was re-signed can keep being served by the previous extension even after the app itself updates. Widgets now print their version and build number whenever they render an empty or locked state, which are exactly the states people photograph when reporting a problem. A screenshot is now enough to tell a genuine bug apart from an install that never actually updated, which should make widget reports far quicker to act on. If your widgets are working, you will never see it.

This release fixes three things, all of which were reported rather than found. First, the Lock Screen widget. Since iOS 17 the system will not render a widget that never declares its background, and it substitutes a grey card reading "Please adopt containerBackground API" in its place. Every Home Screen size in Octave declared one; none of the three Lock Screen sizes did. That is the whole reason the widget looked fine on the Home Screen and broken on the Lock Screen, and why the rectangular Lock Screen widget had in fact never worked since the day it shipped. All three Lock Screen sizes now declare a background, as Apple's own documentation requires even though the system removes it there. Second, launching Octave from a web link — a Handoff from Safari on a Mac is the easy way to hit this — could show "Import Failed: that theme couldn't be read" about something that was never a theme. The URL router handed any address it didn't recognise to the theme importer, which downloaded it and tried to parse it as JSON. Only genuine theme files are treated as themes now, and anything unrecognised is ignored. Third, and found while fixing the second: links copied from the theme gallery were built correctly but had no route on the receiving end, so opening one did nothing at all. Shared theme links now open the theme they point at.

This release is about the Home Screen widgets, which had quietly become the worst-looking part of Octave. All six have been rebuilt. The previous versions drew their own black background and tinted it with the current album's accent colour, so every widget was the same muddy maroon regardless of what was playing. Worse, they used the system's semantic secondary text colour on top of it — and that colour is computed for the system's background, not one an app paints itself, so artist names, section headers and timestamps were rendering at nearly the same brightness as the surface behind them. They are now built on the standard iOS widget material and nothing else. The semantic colours are correct by construction, light mode works, and on iOS 26 the system renders the widgets as Liquid Glass and applies the tinted and clear Home Screen treatments without Octave doing anything. Album artwork is the only colour left in a widget, and it deliberately stays full colour even in tinted mode, because a desaturated album cover is unrecognisable. The list widgets also spread their rows across the full height instead of bunching them under the header and leaving a dead band at the bottom. Now Playing picked up the circular and inline Lock Screen sizes, so it can be a progress ring or a one-line status as well as the rectangular card. Separately, a long-standing artwork bug is fixed: when the catalogue retires a cover it does not return an error, it redirects to a blank grey disc and serves it as a valid image, so Octave showed that disc as if it were the album art. Retired covers are now detected and replaced with Octave's own placeholder, in the app and in the widgets alike.

Tapping Download on a long list could end with one song being attempted again and again, its progress climbing to 100%, dropping to 90%, climbing back and then failing, while everything behind it sat waiting. Almost none of that was the track being difficult. Downloads are tagged as they stream — Octave writes the title, artist and cover art into the file on the way past — and a streamed reply loses the header that states how many bytes are coming. That one missing number caused most of this. Progress had to be estimated from the song's length and bitrate, which for anything not encoded at a constant rate reads 100% while bytes are still arriving. A connection that died part-way through ended the transfer cleanly enough to look finished, so a half-written song was saved to your library with a real entry, played as far as it got, and was then found short by the next launch's integrity check, deleted and fetched again — the other half of why downloads appeared to repeat themselves indefinitely. And because nothing identified the file, an interrupted download could not be continued: it began again at byte one, so a connection bad enough to break a large lossless track once broke the retry too, and after a few attempts the song was written off. All of that is fixed. The real size is sent with every download and checked against what lands, so a short file is a failed attempt that gets retried rather than a saved song that is quietly broken. Interrupted downloads resume from the byte they reached instead of starting over. The progress bar adds up genuine progress and never moves backwards. And when the servers say a particular track cannot be served for the next quarter of an hour, Octave stops holding the download open waiting on it — it parks that song, finishes the rest of the list, and tells you at the end which one it could not get.

Downloading Liked Songs could end with the same song being retried on a loop. Each track was allowed a few attempts before Octave gave up on it, but giving up left no record anywhere: a song that never finished was never marked as saved, so the next time anything looked at your library it looked like work that had not been started yet and was handed a fresh set of attempts. Smart Downloads checks your Liked Songs when the app opens, when you turn the setting on, and every couple of hours in the background, and each of those checks skips every song already on your phone — which means it re-queued exactly the one song that could not be saved, and only that one. Long after the rest of the list was safely downloaded, the queue was a single track being attacked over and over. Octave now remembers when it has given up on something and leaves it alone for fifteen minutes, then longer if it keeps failing, while still picking it up by itself once the problem clears. Tapping Download on that song, or on the collection a second time, still forces an immediate retry, because asking for something twice should mean something. Retries also go to the back of the queue instead of the front, so one difficult track can no longer push ahead of the hundreds waiting behind it. And a download that fails now says so when the run ends, instead of the progress panel quietly disappearing. Separately, on the web player, Safari was silently refusing to keep offline copies at all — the file downloaded but nothing was stored, so the Downloaded list stayed empty behind a Restore button that could never succeed. That is fixed for iPhone and Mac Safari alike.

3.1 fixed the reason Home-Screen widgets were empty for almost everyone — the App Group identifier that lets the app and its widgets share data is unique across every Apple developer account, so a copy signed with your own Apple ID is issued a different one and the app was still writing to the name it was compiled with. That release stopped hardcoding the name and went looking for it instead, but it could only look for names it had been told to expect, which meant guessing at how Sideloadly, AltStore and SideStore each construct one. This release removes the guess. A tool that renames the group must request a provisioning profile for the new name, and that profile is shipped inside the app it signs, so Octave now reads the granted identifier directly out of it and both halves agree no matter what the tool chose. The guesses are kept only as a fallback for builds that carry no profile at all, where the original name is already the right answer. Nothing else changed: where the signature grants no App Group whatsoever, Top Charts, Discover and Live Radio still load from our servers instead of rendering blank, and the three that read your library still say what is actually wrong rather than telling you to open an app that would change nothing.

A release about the widgets, and about never having to hunt for a download again. Home-Screen widgets were empty for almost everybody, and the reason is a detail of how Apple hands out App Groups: the identifier that lets an app and its widget share data is unique across every developer account on earth, so ours belongs permanently to us. When you re-sign the app with your own Apple ID — which is what Sideloadly, AltStore and SideStore all do — you are issued a different identifier, or on a free account none at all, while the app carried on writing to the name it was compiled with. The two halves were reading and writing different boxes. Octave now works out which App Group it was actually given at launch and both halves use that one, so widgets fill in the way they always did on our own builds. Where the signature grants no App Group whatsoever, Top Charts, Discover and Live Radio no longer sit blank — none of the three needs anything from your phone, so they load from Octave's servers directly. Now Playing, Recently Played and Pins do need your library and cannot work around it; instead of telling you to open an app that would change nothing, they now say what is actually wrong. Separately, Octave is an AltStore source: paste octavestreaming.com/apps.json into AltStore, SideStore, Feather or TrollApps and it appears as a listing with every version and its notes, and future releases arrive as an in-app update rather than a file you go and fetch. Every past build is in there too, and the old download links still resolve.

An artwork release, and the reason it's a whole number. The player had been drawing a second copy of the album cover behind the first — scaled up and heavily blurred — and dissolving the real cover halfway down the screen so the two could meet without a visible seam. That is why the whole player read as out of focus, and why the subject of a photograph was so often eaten by the fade. Both layers are gone. Albums that ship a portrait or animated cover now fill the screen with it, cropped to where the picture genuinely ends rather than to the empty space some posters carry underneath; everything else gets the cover as a card resting on the album's own colours, which is what a square sleeve wants to be. The cover also breathes now — it eases smaller when you pause and springs back when you play. Separately, covers stopped being the wrong album: higher-resolution artwork was found by searching the artist and album as plain text and accepting the first result, verifying only that the artist looked about right, which is precisely the case a wrong answer passes — Belle and Sebastian's "Books" came back with the sleeve for "If You're Feeling Sinister", and of fifteen albums checked, nine resolved to the wrong record. Matches are now confirmed against the album too, and an unconfirmed one keeps the original cover instead of guessing. Colour follows the same rule: it is read from the picture on screen rather than from the square sleeve, so an animated cover no longer tints the screen with a different photograph's palette, and a sleeve that is a small poster on a wide cream border is read from the poster rather than washing out to grey. Album pages could also show a different edition's cover entirely, because a barcode is not unique at Apple and we took whichever edition was listed first — that now picks the edition you're actually looking at. Finally, the mini player can be opened by VoiceOver, which it could not before.

Sing finally sounds like karaoke. Until now it worked by cancelling whatever sits in the centre of the mix, which is where the lead vocal lives — but so do the kick, the snare and the bass, so the song came out thin, and on an older or narrower mix the voice barely moved at all. Songs that have been through our vocal separation now play a properly separated backing track instead. Measured against the original it removes about 9dB from the range a lead vocal occupies while leaving the bass within 2dB of where it started, and unlike the old method it works on mono and on wide mixes, both of which used to defeat it. The fader still does what it did: push it most of the way up and the voice is gone, ease it back and the singer sits quietly underneath so you can follow the next line. Those are two different jobs and they're now done two different ways — the separated track for “gone”, the original for “quiet” — with the app moving between them as you drag, and never running both at once. An HD badge appears above the fader when the song you're on has a separated backing track, because not every song does yet and the two are different enough to hear.

An audio release — three things people said sounded wrong, and all three were real. Bass-heavy songs distorted with the EQ on: the EQ's bands are wide enough to overlap, so Bass Boost's “+7dB” was really producing about +13dB, and everything past the ceiling was being chopped flat rather than turned down — that's a clipper, and on a track where the sub-bass carries the waveform it's the crackle you were hearing. The EQ now measures every block of audio it's about to play and backs off by however much it's actually over, so a boosted preset stays a boost. Volume levelling was only ever turning songs down, so a loud modern master came down to meet a quiet older one while the quiet one stayed put and the difference between them survived; it now works in both directions. It was also only running while the visualiser was on screen — so for anyone who never opened it, the feature did nothing at all — and it was measuring raw energy rather than perceived loudness, which reads bass-heavy mixes as louder than they sound. It now measures the way ears do, on every song, whether or not anything is on screen. And songs stopped jumping to the next track about three quarters of the way through, or restarting there with repeat on. The app looks for a fade-out so it can mix out of the last real note instead of into silence, but it was reading that from whatever audio had reached the phone, and a download that stopped early looks identical to a song that goes quiet early. It won't call something a fade-out now unless it has heard the whole song, it won't accept more than 20 seconds as a tail, and it no longer shares that reading with everyone else — so one interrupted download can't skip songs on other people's phones.

A correctness and performance release, most of it from things people reported directly. Swiping left on a song in a playlist queues it instead of playing it — the row slides under your finger, so your thumb never left the button underneath and the tap fired on release. A whole album can now be added to a playlist, from the album page or from any album cover, including straight into a brand-new playlist named after it; before this, an album could be queued but never filed. Very large playlists no longer stall the app or heat the phone: a 1,500-song playlist was re-sorting, re-reading and re-scanning itself on every update, roughly three times a frame's budget of work each time, and now does that once and reuses it. Your own imported files finally behave like songs — they can go in playlists, be liked, and show in Recently Played, and they survive a reinstall; they had been lumped in with live radio and podcast episodes. The playlist importer accepts the formats it advertises, so M3U and XSPF exports are no longer greyed out in the file picker. Transitions are cleaner on AirPlay and Bluetooth when you connect a speaker mid-blend. The mini player's play, skip and like targets meet Apple's minimum size without looking any different, and the account button now announces itself properly to VoiceOver instead of reading out an icon name. Under the hood the app measures its own performance on real devices from now on, so problems like the playlist one surface without waiting for someone to report them.

A repair release built from what people actually reported. Playlists and albums scroll properly again — a drag that began on a song was being taken by the row rather than the list, so it neither swiped nor scrolled and only the very edge of the screen worked. Long playlists stopped stuttering: every frame of a scroll was rebuilding the entire track list, and on a big playlist the queue was being rebuilt once per visible row on top of that. Search filters return results — setting any duration or tempo filter previously returned nothing for every query, including exact titles. Downloads work on a fresh install, where the first ones were being built before the playback key arrived, rejected, and never retried. Songs resolve to the right album instead of whichever pressing was listed first, which was often a live cut or a greatest-hits disc, and a cold track can no longer spend half a minute hunting for a source. Imports now tell you exactly which songs couldn't be found, as a list you can copy, and a Spotify link that Spotify refuses to share with apps says so plainly instead of claiming the playlist is empty. New: Your Mix, built from everything you listen to and seeded with music you haven't heard yet; Apple's full hand-ranked Top Songs and Essentials playlists on artist pages; cinematic artist videos with the page colour taken from the clip; suggested songs at the end of a playlist; and sorting a playlist by title, artist, album or date added without touching your own order.

Update for the crash: adding a song to a playlist took the whole app down, every time, and that's fixed. Wireless playback got the next-biggest repair — transitions were stretching the incoming song's tempo and nudging its speed several times a second, which the phone's own output handles fine but a HomePod, car stereo or Bluetooth speaker turns into crackling and tracks that seem to skip themselves; over those routes it now falls back to a short clean fade. Sing was taking the band with the singer, because the kick, bass and snare sit dead-centre in a mix just like a lead vocal does — it now removes the voice and puts the low end and the cymbals back, and you'll hear the difference on the first song you try. Podcasts are rebuilt on Apple's catalogue: the full curated browse page, real categories, search that reaches inside shows to find episodes, and hosts, listener reviews, trailers and "listeners also subscribed" on every show. Collaborative playlists can now be ended, and once one is, everyone in the room can save it to their library, pin it or download it as their own copy. A song the catalogue can't serve no longer sits on a spinner forever — it's skipped after a few seconds, and you pick how many in Settings. And lyrics get two options that were web-only: hide the per-line share button so long lines use the full width, and choose whether the active line animates.

A polish pass over 2.5. Opening Now Playing no longer starts low and snaps upward — the player was deciding between its two artwork layouts after the animation had already finished, and the cover was staying tucked under the status bar for the whole travel; both are now settled before the first frame. Swiping up on the player does nothing at all, as it should, and swiping down still dismisses. Animated covers stop forgetting they are animated: scrolling past enough of them could quietly kill the one you were actually looking at, leaving the still image behind. Recently Played's All songs / Favourites / Downloads chips shrink to icons so the row stops overflowing, and Clear history is just a bin. Reordering Liked Songs finally matches what you are looking at — dragging a song to the top no longer sends it to the bottom. The lyric share card gets a much bigger cover, breathing room around the quote mark, and a wordmark that isn't hidden behind the buttons. Album pages get the overflow menu they were missing (Play Next, Add to Queue, Suggest Less, Copy Link). And the app now honours the system Larger Text setting, which it had never done anywhere.

The parity release — everything the web player can do, the iPhone app now does too. Now Playing was rebuilt around a single continuous movement: the artwork travels between the mini player and the full screen instead of cross-fading, and you can catch the swipe halfway and throw it back. Albums with motion artwork play it full-screen behind the player and on the Lock Screen. The whole Apple Music editorial layer landed — Made For You, Apple Radio, editorial charts, curated playlists and artist spotlights — alongside a rebuilt Browse and Discover with real curated artwork (and no more washed-out, over-blurred tiles). Listening Parties let a room hear the same song at the same moment; collaborative playlists let people build one together; public profiles let you share what you've made. Plus Concerts for artists you follow, Stats and a shareable Wrapped recap, dedicated Radio and Podcasts hubs, and a search with proper filter chips, a top result and browsable genre pages. Shared links now open the right screen instead of dropping you on the home tab. And it should cost you less battery: animations, visualisers and motion artwork stand down on their own under Low Power Mode or when the phone runs warm.

privacy.NSMicrophoneUsageDescription: Octave uses the microphone for voice search.
privacy.NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription: Octave uses speech recognition so you can search by voice.
privacy.NSPhotoLibraryAddUsageDescription: Octave saves shareable song images to your photo library.
privacy.NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription: Octave uses your approximate location once to find concerts happening near you. It is never stored or shared.

apps.versionDescription: The first play of a song nobody had played yet failed on iPhone: the server sent the whole file without honouring the byte ranges iOS asks for, and iOS refuses that for lossless, Atmos and AAC files. The server now answers those requests the way iOS expects, so a never-played song starts in a few seconds instead of failing. Worse, after one failure like that the player itself could stop accepting songs — even files already on your phone — until the app was quit; it is now replaced with a fresh one the moment it holds a failed song, and a player that says "playing" while holding nothing is rebuilt within seconds at the same position. A failed switch to Dolby Atmos or to a new quality no longer skips the song that was playing fine, the connections used for playback time out and are rebuilt after a long idle or a switch between Wi-Fi and cellular, and the next song no longer tries to preload before your playback token is ready. Next and Previous now change the title, artwork and lock screen on the tap and silence the old song straight away; with AutoMix on, the next song is preloaded again. Covers are downloaded once per song, retried when a connection drops, fetched through Octave's servers when Apple's or Deezer's image servers refuse, and loaded again as soon as the network or the app comes back — a cover that fails no longer leaves the previous song's cover in its place. Downloads keep going through iOS dropping the download service, force-quits and brief previews, with longer pauses between retries. Add a folder uses Apple's folder picker, reads the folder the way Apple documents, downloads songs still in iCloud first, and says what went wrong when it can't.
